section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Puzzle and the Binary Odometer
section_1.content: Introduce the Towers of Hanoi rules (3 pegs, move one disk at a time, never place larger on smaller). Simultaneously, introduce a 3-bit binary counter (000 to 111). Explain that the number of moves required is 2^n - 1.
section_1.example: Visualize a robotic arm 'Alpha' standing before 3 golden disks. Beside the arm, a digital screen displays binary numbers starting at 000.

section_2.title: The Mapping: Disks as Bit Positions
section_2.content: Establish a one-to-one relationship: The 'k-th' bit of a binary number corresponds to the 'k-th' disk. The rightmost bit (Bit 1) represents the smallest disk, the second bit represents the medium disk, and so on.
section_2.example: Color-code the disks: Disk 1 (Smallest/Red), Disk 2 (Medium/Green), Disk 3 (Largest/Blue). Map these to binary positions: [Bit3:Blue][Bit2:Green][Bit1:Red].

section_3.title: The Rule of the Changing Bit
section_3.content: Introduce the core logic: In each step of binary counting, identify which bit *flips* to change the value. The position of the rightmost bit that flips tells you exactly which disk to move.
section_3.example: Moving from 000 to 001: The 1st bit flips, so move Disk 1. Moving from 001 to 010: The 2nd bit is the rightmost to flip (01 is replaced by 10), so move Disk 2.

section_4.title: Step-by-Step Execution: 1 to 7
section_4.content: Execute the sequence of binary increments. 1 (001) -> Move Disk 1. 2 (010) -> Move Disk 2. 3 (011) -> Move Disk 1. 4 (100) -> Move Disk 3. This rhythmic pattern reveals a fractal-like symmetry.
section_4.example: Show a split-screen animation. Left side: Binary counter increments with the changing bit highlighted in yellow. Right side: The corresponding disk glides to a new peg in real-time.

section_5.title: The 'Where to Move' Directional Logic
section_5.content: Explain how to determine the destination peg. For an odd number of disks: Move Disk 1 in a cycle (Peg A -> C -> B). For even disks: (Peg A -> B -> C). All other disks simply move to the only available legal spot.
section_5.example: A compass graphic appears. For our 3-disk (odd) setup, Disk 1 always follows a 'Clockwise' path (Peg 1 to 3, 3 to 2, 2 to 1), while other disks follow the logic of the only legal move.

section_6.title: Conclusion: The Elegance of Binary Structure
section_6.content: Summarize how the binary number system inherently contains the recursive solution to the Towers of Hanoi. This demonstrates that mathematical patterns often govern physical constraints.
section_6.example: The binary counter reaches 111 (7 moves), and all disks are perfectly stacked on the final peg. The robot 'Alpha' powers down as the binary sequence fades into a tree-diagram showing the recursive nature of the moves.
